Insurance reimbursement and cash flow: a covered expense can still need money upfront

Four graphics connect recognized claims, a remaining deductible, an insurer-payment maximum and the cash needed before receipts arrive.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore expenses before insurance reimbursements arrive

Hypothetical private-benefit claims, not a public dental/health-program or insurer quote. Identical invoices arrive at the start of consecutive months in one benefit year. Recognized amount is capped at invoice value; remaining deductible is applied first, then the coverage percentage, then the remaining insurer-payment maximum. No maximum reset occurs. Claim m pays at the end of month m + delay, even at zero delay. Other budget surplus arrives at month-end. The model runs through claim months + delay and measures shortages immediately after bills, before receipts. The central idea

The eventual amount reimbursed and the cash needed to pay invoices answer different questions. Track both the benefit calculation and the timing of bills and receipts.

01

Separate the invoice, recognized amount and insurer payment

The FCAC’s health-insurance guide highlights that a policy may pay only a percentage of a claim or impose a maximum annual amount. The actual contract determines what is covered and how a claim is assessed.

This illustration assumes approved private-benefit claims and uses an explicit calculation order: cap the recognized amount at the invoice, apply the remaining deductible, apply the insurer’s percentage, then apply the remaining insurer-payment maximum.

Those are hypothetical contract conventions, not rules for every plan. The tool calculates neither eligibility nor a public dental or health-program benefit. The number and size of invoices are financial assumptions, rather than a recommendation about treatment or clinical need.

02

Follow the remaining deductible and maximum through the claims

The default schedule has a CAD 600 invoice at the start of each of six consecutive months in one benefit year. CAD 500 per invoice is recognized. The remaining deductible starts at CAD 100, the insurer percentage is 80%, and the remaining insurer-payment maximum is CAD 1,500.

For the first claim, CAD 500 less CAD 100 leaves CAD 400 to which the 80% share applies. The modeled reimbursement is CAD 320. The next two claims reimburse CAD 400 each. Only CAD 380 remains under the payment maximum for the fourth claim.

The fifth and sixth invoices still cost CAD 600 each, but the maximum has been exhausted and their modeled reimbursements are zero. Total invoices are CAD 3,600, total reimbursement is CAD 1,500, and the unreimbursed cost is CAD 2,100. The bars show why a headline 80% share does not mean 80% of every invoice is paid.

03

Place cash receipts after the invoices that generate them

Every invoice is paid at the start of its month. A two-month receipt delay means the first claim, from month one, is reimbursed at the end of month three. Even zero full-month delay means month-end payment in this model, rather than payment at the provider’s counter.

The household also contributes CAD 150 of other budget surplus at each month-end. That amount is assumed available after regular household costs and premiums, before the invoices shown here. It must not include a reimbursement that is already entered elsewhere in the schedule.

The default starts with CAD 1,500 allocated cash. After the month-three invoice, cash reaches zero before the later month-end resources arrive. After the month-four invoice it reaches negative CAD 130, although that month ends positive at CAD 420. A positive month-end observation can therefore hide an earlier funding need.

04

Use the deepest shortage to measure starting cash needs

The lowest default position after an invoice is negative CAD 230 in month six. The starting amount needed for the entire schedule is CAD 1,730, or CAD 230 beyond the selected reserve. A negative chart point represents an unfunded need, not an approved overdraft.

The model continues through invoice months plus receipt delay, so all assumed claims have a receipt date within the horizon. With the selected monthly surplus, the default ledger ends month eight at positive CAD 600. That eventual balance does not remove the earlier shortage.

The receipt-delay bars keep invoices and eventual reimbursement unchanged. Under the defaults, zero full-month delay requires CAD 1,350 at the start, while four months requires CAD 2,530. Timing can change liquidity needs without changing the eventual benefit amount.

05

Check the timing assumption as well as the coverage percentage

The matrix varies the insurer share and receipt delay. Recognized costs, deductible, payment maximum, invoice count, budget surplus and starting cash stay selected. Different percentages can produce the same eventual payment when the maximum binds.

All invoices are assigned to one benefit year, with no maximum reset. The model excludes direct billing, a second plan, claim disputes, premiums, tax credits and borrowing costs. Actual reimbursement dates and contract ordering need confirmation before using a schedule for real payments.

The four graphics keep ultimate cost and temporary cash needs visible together. A practical review records the invoice amount and due date, the confirmed benefit calculation, the expected receipt date and the source that funds the interval.
